source_text:
τοῦ δὲ πρώτου
παραιτησαμένου προσῆλθεν ὁ πατὴρ τῷ δευτέρῳ, τοῦτ' ἔστιν τῷ Ἰσραήλ, ὅστις
καλούμενος διὰ Μωυσέως εἶπεν· «πάντα ὅσα ἐλάλησεν « ὁ θεὸς καὶ «ποιήσομεν καὶ
ἀκουσόμεθα «. οἵτινες οὔτε ἐποίησαν οὔτε ἤκουσαν οὔτε μετεμελήθησαν ὕστερον.
οὓς κατέκριναν αἱ πόρναι καὶ οἱ τελῶναι, τοῦτ' ἔστιν τὰ ἔθνη.
thought_title: The second son's refusal and the Gentiles' condemnation
orientation: Theophilus is explaining the parable of the two sons in Matthew 21:28–32, and has just described the first son, the Gentiles, who repented and went into the vineyard.
pass_a_gloss: And when the first had refused, the father went to the second, that is to Israel, who, being called through Moses, said: "All things that God spoke, and we will do and we will hear." Who neither did nor heard nor repented afterward. Whom the prostitutes and the tax collectors condemned, that is the Gentiles.

choices.why: The aorist middle participle indicates the first son's completed act of declining the father's call, matching the parable's 'I will not'.
The verb means to approach or come to someone; 'went to' preserves the father's initiative in calling the second son.
The passive participle with διὰ indicates the means by which Israel was called, preserving the instrumental sense of Moses as mediator.
The aorist passive of μεταμέλομαι means to regret or change one's mind afterward; 'repented' matches the glossary sense and the contrast with the first son's later repentance.
The aorist active of κατακρίνω means to judge against or condemn; the prostitutes and tax collectors are the subject who condemn Israel by their repentance.

bible_refs.note: πάντα ὅσα ἐλάλησεν ὁ θεὸς καὶ ποιήσομεν καὶ ἀκουσόμεθα

pass_b_english: When the first son—the Gentiles—had refused, the Father went to the second son—that is, to Israel—who, being called through Moses, said, “All that God has spoken, we will do and we will hear.” But they neither did nor heard, nor did they repent afterward. The prostitutes and the tax collectors—that is, the Gentiles—condemned them.

problems.quote: The prostitutes and the tax collectors—that is, the Gentiles—condemned them
problems.source_quote: οὓς κατέκριναν αἱ πόρναι καὶ οἱ τελῶναι, τοῦτ' ἔστιν τὰ ἔθνη
problems.why: The Greek says the prostitutes and tax collectors condemned Israel (οὓς = Israel as object), but the English structure makes 'the prostitutes and tax collectors' the subject and 'them' the object, which reverses agency: it sounds like Gentiles condemned Israel, when the point is that repentant outcasts (identified as Gentiles) passed judgment on/condemned Israel by their better response.
problems.fix: These were condemned by the prostitutes and tax collectors—that is, the Gentiles

problems.source_quote: «πάντα ὅσα ἐλάλησεν ὁ θεὸς καὶ ποιήσομεν καὶ ἀκουσόμεθα»
problems.why: The quotation echoes Exodus 19:8 and 24:3, 7, but the source marks it as Israel's speech, not a direct OT citation. The brief says OT quotations should use LXX book names where identifiable; more importantly, the source presents this as the second son's spoken response, not as a formal scripture citation. The parenthetical (Exodus 24:7) is an editorial addition not in the source.
problems.fix: Remove the parenthetical citation, or if kept, note it as composite/allusion.
problems.ruling: Source has no scripture reference; '(Exodus 24:7)' is an editorial addition not in the Greek text, misleading readers.

last_rejected.quote: When the first son—the Gentiles—had refused
last_rejected.why: This clause names only the first son as having refused. It does not identify him as the Gentiles.
last_rejected.fix: When the first son had refused, the Father went to the second son—that is, to Israel—
last_rejected.ruling: The insertion 'the Gentiles' is not in 'τοῦ δὲ πρώτου παραιτησαμένου'. But the parallel 'τῷ δευτέρῳ, τοῦτ' ἔστιν τῷ Ἰσραήλ' and the closing 'τὰ ἔθνη' imply it, so no reader is misled.
